clue.text: Suffering rejection by relatives joins husband for Islamic wedding

indicators.note: the relatives undergo a rejection, which turns their word back to front

parts.note: kin are one's relatives
by in the sense of per, as in 'three a day', gives A

explanation.surface: Someone spurned by their family marries anyway in an Islamic ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suffering rejection' turns KIN into NIK; 'by' gives A through its sense of per ('so much a head').
explanation.definitionFit: This Arabic-derived term names the marriage contract and ceremony in Islamic law.

clue.text: Hopeless faux pas by player in eastern drama

indicators.note: the player's blunder sits inside the drama's word

parts.note: No (or Noh) is the classical Japanese masked drama
an own goal, OG, is a footballer's embarrassing blunder

explanation.surface: An actor's clumsy blunder during a Japanese play leaves the show hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests an actor in the drama, but it is a footballer, whose faux pas is an own goal (OG).
explanation.definitionFit: A situation described as a non-starter is hopeless, the informal idiom for something impossible.

clue.text: A big piece of luck in golf

indicators.note: piece of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A big stroke of luck on the golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piece of' picks out the letters running across 'luCK IN Golf'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a prefix-like adjective, as in a royal-sized bed, the word means outsize or very large.

clue.text: Occupants of sea shanty having a little party

indicators.note: the shanty holds the other pieces within it

parts.note: a shanty is a crude shack or hut
LIB is a short form of the Liberal party

explanation.surface: Sailors singing sea shanties enjoy a small celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea shanty' reads as a song, but 'shanty' is a hut; 'little party' is Lib, short for Liberal.
explanation.definitionFit: These large flatfish live in the sea; the plural noun of the species doubles as the singular.

clue.text: Stars I bet he'll treat suspiciously

indicators.note: a suspicious handling of the phrase stirs its letters into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone bets that a person will treat stars warily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspiciously' rearranges the whole run 'I bet he'll treat'; Ursa Minor is the constellation meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursa Minor, the constellation containing Polaris, is a group of stars.

clue.text: In Florida resort to work corruptly for auditor

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so the word is as heard

parts.note: to tamper is to interfere corruptly, as with evidence or a jury

explanation.surface: An auditor in a Florida resort is caught cooking the books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant, but here it is simply a listener; in non-rhotic British speech the two words sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: This Gulf Coast city on its bay is a well-known Floridian holiday destination.

clue.text: A long time in the past a gambling game, never ever forgotten

parts.words: in the past a gambling game
parts.note: E-O was an eighteenth-century gambling game, a forerunner of roulette

indicators.note: the second word is left out of the first

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A long time ago people played a gambling game that is now entirely forgotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forgotten' removes EVER from NEVER, leaving N. E-O (even-odd) was an old casino game.
explanation.definitionFit: An age or aeon is an immensely long period, often used of geological time.

clue.text: Movie-cameras one's keeping cool

indicators.note: one's holds the cameras inside it

parts.note: one is I, and 's adds S
cines are cine cameras used for filming

explanation.surface: Film cameras need to be kept cool to work properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts CINES between I and S.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun meaning coldness or chill; 'cool' works as a noun for a cold state.

clue.text: Smartening it up, repeatedly given a hand but no head

indicators.note: the little word appears twice over
in a down light, up means the doubled word reads bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: an ovation is applause, a hand given to a performer

explanation.surface: Someone tidying up is applauded again and again, though not on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repeatedly' makes ITIT and 'up' turns it to TITI; 'no head' drops O from OVATION to leave VATION.
explanation.definitionFit: Titivating is making oneself smart, so the noun means the act of smartening or prinking.

clue.text: Teacher's briefly taken lunch outside — they're on roll

indicators.note: the shortened meal word goes around the teacher
the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: having taken lunch, one has eaten
a lector is a university teacher; the 's is 'is', a link

explanation.surface: A teacher grabs a quick lunch outside while the pupils are on the register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll' looks like a bread roll beside 'lunch', but it is the electoral roll; a lector is a university reader or teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Voters are listed on the electoral register, so the whole body of voters is those on the roll.

clue.text: Elegant, refined male accepted by nobility at the outset

definitions.text: Elegant, refined male accepted by nobility at the outset

indicators.note: the male letter is taken into the rearranged word
refining reworks the letters into a new form
only the start of the word is used

explanation.surface: A polished man is welcomed into high society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refined' rearranges ELEGANT to GENTLEA, which takes M inside; then N, the start of 'nobility', closes it. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cultivated, courteous man of good breeding is just what the whole clue portrays.

clue.text: Hitmen shot outside Exeter rehabilitated, remarkably

indicators.note: the first rearranged group wraps around the second
shot as in broken or ruined, so the letters are jumbled
rehabilitating remakes the city's letters in a new order

explanation.surface: Gunmen shot around Exeter are reformed, astonishingly.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate anagrams, one wrapped round the other: the first rearranged group splits so its last two letters fall after the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to the highest degree, much as 'remarkably' intensifies an adjective.

clue.text: East End journo's split level TV ruined by bloody drink

parts.note: B is the euphemistic stand-in for the swear word, as in 'b----y'

indicators.note: the journalist's word cuts into the jumbled letters
ruined letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: East End Cockney speech drops the initial H

parts.note: a hack is a journalist; the 's is a link

explanation.surface: A Cockney reporter's split-level television is ruined by a spilt drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' makes LVELVET of the fodder; the East End of London is famous for dropping H's, so the journalist loses his first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cocktail of stout and champagne, a classic mixed drink named for its dark smoothness.

clue.text: Flew alien over in hoax

indicators.note: the turned alien goes inside the hoax

parts.note: to kid is to hoax or fool someone

indicators.note: in a down light, over turns the word upside down

parts.note: ET is the film extraterrestrial

explanation.surface: An alien flew over as part of a hoax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoax' is a verb here, to kid; 'over' turns the alien upside down in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: To fly a kite past tense, or more loosely to soar like a kite; a verb in the past tense.

clue.text: Bard, looking sickly in Seat 5, willing to participate

indicators.note: the pale word goes inside the seat

parts.note: a sofa is a long seat
wan means pale and sickly-looking
V is the Roman numeral five
if you're on for something, you're willing to take part

explanation.surface: The Bard looks pale in seat number 5 but is keen to take part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat 5' looks like a seat number, but the seat and the numeral are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Jonson's epithet for Shakespeare, born at Stratford upon the river Avon, the Bard.

clue.text: Claim from hypochondriac's won round writer

indicators.note: the winning word goes around the hypochondriac's claim

parts.note: taken as written
a hypochondriac claims 'ill I am', with the 's adding S

explanation.surface: A writer won his case by claiming to be a hypochondriac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts W...ON around ILL I AM'S. The 's adds an S here rather than being a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Williamson was the English novelist who wrote Tarka the Otter.

clue.text: Winding in and out of Ascot Henry covered up with a garment

indicators.note: the letters wind through each other, mixing into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the letter is hidden away, so it drops out

parts.note: H is the henry, the SI unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Someone weaves through Ascot racecourse with Henry, covered up in a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covered up' removes H from WITH A, leaving WITA, whose letters 'winding in and out of' ASCOT alternate with it. Ascot is the English racecourse famed for dressing up.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleeveless vest worn over a shirt and under a jacket is an item of clothing.

clue.text: Work at expanding crossword compilers' repute

indicators.note: the possessive pronoun swells to take the work inside

parts.note: setters call themselves 'we', so the compilers' is ours
to do something is to work at it

explanation.surface: Working at expanding the reputation of crossword setters.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters speak of themselves as 'we', so 'crossword compilers'' gives the possessive pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in good or bad odour with someone means having good or bad standing, so it means reputation.

clue.text: Orang-utan? It's being bellicose

parts.note: It is slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
Tyr is the Norse god of war, a warlike being

explanation.surface: A great ape is in a fighting mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' is SA plus a link 'is'; 'It' means sex appeal. The question mark flags the obscure sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Old naturalists used the woodland-demigod name for the orang-utan, a sense dictionaries still record.

clue.text: Something fruity you've the good sense to remove from wine-list

indicators.note: the good sense is taken out of the drinks menu

parts.note: wit means intelligence or good sense

explanation.surface: A wine waiter has the sense to take a fruity bottle off the list.
explanation.walkthrough: W, I and T are taken out of WINELIST in order, though not side by side, leaving the pear variety.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a winter pear, an obscure fruit known chiefly to crossword solvers.

clue.text: How judge operates? Utterly British, and not a minute too soon?

parts.note: so means utterly, as in 'so tired'

indicators.note: the single letter is removed

parts.note: a minute early is too soon

explanation.surface: A judge is utterly British and arrives just in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a' removes A from EARLY, leaving ERLY. The definition plays on the saying 'sober as a judge'.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'sober as a judge' means a judge proceeds in a serious, restrained way.

clue.text: Those excluded from adult learning facility getting into a scrap

indicators.note: the university goes inside the scrap

parts.note: an oddment is a leftover scrap
OU is the Open University, which teaches adults by distance learning

explanation.surface: Those left out of an adult education centre end up in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' suggests a fight but means a leftover. The OU is Britain's Open University.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes people who don't fit in with the rest, so they stand excluded.

clue.text: See 10
"Fat" Alban canonised? Blow me down!

parts.note: flab is body fat
Alban Berg was the Austrian composer
a canonised person has been made a saint, giving A and ST

explanation.surface: Someone is astonished that a fat man named Alban has been made a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alban' looks like St Alban the martyr, but it is Alban Berg.
explanation.definitionFit: Both express being astounded; the exclamation means 'that amazes me', the verb means to astonish.

clue.text: Finally reducing support for the head

indicators.note: the phrase is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: at last means finally

explanation.surface: A neck brace finally eases the strain on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reducing' drops the last T from AT LAST.
explanation.definitionFit: The topmost vertebra, named after the Titan who held up the sky, carries the skull.

clue.text: See 4 across
Given the odds, it's easy for old Gordon Bennett!

indicators.note: only the odd-numbered letters of the phrase are used

explanation.surface: A bookie scoffs that, at these odds, winning is easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given the odds' keeps letters 1, 3, 5 and 7 of ITSEASY. 'Gordon Bennett!' is a dated British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are old-fashioned British exclamations of surprise or mild indignation.

clue.text: On top of ventail is alternative protection

indicators.note: only the leading letter of the word is used

parts.note: taken as written
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A helmet's ventail is topped by a further layer of protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top of' picks V from 'ventail', the lower faceguard of a medieval helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: A helmet's face guard or a cap's peak shields the eyes or face, a form of protection.

clue.text: What asthmatic carries about drug in the interest of hepatologist?

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: the drug goes inside the organs

parts.note: a hepatologist specialises in livers
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: A liver specialist asks what drug an asthma sufferer carries.
explanation.walkthrough: E is the usual crossword drug, ecstasy; the hepatologist's interest is the organ he treats, in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthma sufferers carry inhalers that ease attacks, and these are known by that plural noun.

clue.text: Completely dry up? Unlikely for this feature

definitions.text: Completely dry up? Unlikely for this feature

indicators.note: in a down light, up means the word reads bottom to top

parts.note: to air laundry is to dry it

explanation.surface: A coastal inlet is unlikely ever to dry up completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns AIR into the answer. A drowned river valley is flooded by the sea, so it will hardly dry out.
explanation.definitionFit: A coastal inlet formed by a drowned river valley holds seawater, so it can scarcely run dry.

clue.text: Period Poles span in merging organs?

indicators.note: the two poles reach across the middle pieces

parts.note: N and S are the north and south poles
taken as written
eye and ear merged, sharing one E

explanation.surface: A spell of time when Polish people bridge merging body parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' suggests Polish people but means the north and south poles; the two organs share one E when merged.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine years is a span of time, so it counts as a period.

clue.text: Like bird enjoying breakfast in the garden, not quite topless

definitions.text: Like bird enjoying breakfast in the garden

indicators.note: the first letter is taken off

parts.note: nearly means not quite

explanation.surface: A bird eating breakfast outside, almost without a top on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' drops N from NEARLY. The definition alludes to 'the early bird catches the worm'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb's bird that rises first gets the worm, a breakfast in the garden.
